text:
Predicates:
Employee(x) ::: x is an employee.
ScheduleMeeting(x) ::: x schedules a meeting with their customers.
GoToCompany(x) ::: x will go to the company building today.
LunchInCompany(x) ::: x has lunch in the company building.
LunchAtHome(x) ::: x has lunch at home.
WorkRemote(x) ::: x is working remotely from home.
InOtherCountries(x) ::: x is in other countries.
Manager(x) ::: x is a manager.
James ::: James.

Premises:
∀x ((Employee(x) ∧ ScheduleMeeting(x)) → GoToCompany(x)) ::: All employees who schedule a meeting with their customers will go to the company building today.
∀x (LunchInCompany(x) → ScheduleMeeting(x)) ::: Everyone who has lunch in the company building schedules meetings with their customers.
∀x (Employee(x) → (LunchInCompany(x) ∨ LunchAtHome(x))) ::: Employees have lunch either in the company building or at home.
∀x ((Employee(x) ∧ LunchAtHome(x)) → WorkRemote(x)) ::: If an employee has lunch at home, they are working remotely from home.
∀x ((Employee(x) ∧ InOtherCountries(x)) → WorkRemote(x)) ::: All employees who are in other countries work remotely from home.
∀x (Manager(x) → ¬WorkRemote(x)) ::: No managers work remotely from home.
GoToCompany(james) ↔ Manager(james) ::: James will appear in the company today if and only if he is a manager.

Conclusion:
(Manager(james) ∨ InOtherCountries(james)) → ¬(LunchAtHome(james) ∨ WorkRemote(james)) ::: If James is either a manager or in other countries, then James does not either have lunch at home or work remotely from home.
(LunchAtHome(james) ∨ WorkRemote(james)) → ¬(Manager(james) ∨ InOtherCountries(james)) ::: If James either has lunch at home or works remotely from home, then he is neither a manager nor does he work in other countries.
